results.question: How does pod restart policy work?
results.answer: A Pod will not be restarted when the init container image is changed, or the init container completion record has been lost due to garbage collection [1]. The `restartPolicy` for a Pod applies to app containers, and container-level override can be defined [4]. If an init container is created with its `restartPolicy` set to `Always`, it will start and remain running during the entire life of the Pod [4].

results.question: What is the difference between a Deployment and a StatefulSet?
results.answer: StatefulSets are recommended for applications requiring stable network identifiers, persistent storage, ordered deployment and scaling, and automated rolling updates [6]. Deployments provide these features as well, but also offer additional functionality such as being declarative and server-side [4].

results.question: How do init containers differ from sidecar containers?
results.answer: Init containers run to completion before the main application container starts, whereas sidecar containers run concurrently with the main application container [1]. Init containers also do not support probes to control their lifecycle, unlike sidecar containers [4]. Additionally, init containers cannot exchange messages with the app container in a Pod and can only share resources through shared volumes [4].

results.question: What are Kubernetes namespaces used for?
results.answer: Namespaces provide a mechanism for isolating groups of resources within a single cluster [1]. They allow for resource quota management between multiple users and can be used to divide cluster resources [2]. Namespaces also enable features such as unique naming, access control, and resource isolation.

results.question: How does a HorizontalPodAutoscaler decide when to scale?
results.answer: The HorizontalPodAutoscaler decides when to scale based on the ratio between desired metric value and current metric value [3]. It uses the formula `desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas × (currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue))` to calculate the new number of replicas. If the ratio is sufficiently close to 1.0, within a configurable tolerance (0.1 by default), no scaling action is taken [3].

results.question: How does quick sort work?
results.answer:
QuickSort works by selecting a 'pivot' element from the array and partitioning the other elements into two sub-arrays, according to whether they are less than or greater than the pivot. The pivot is then in its correct position in the sorted array [2]. 

In the first pass, QuickSort only guarantees that all elements less than the pivot end up to the left of the pivot, and all elements greater than the pivot end up to the right, with the pivot itself in its correct sorted position [4]. The relative order of these elements is not guaranteed to be sorted.

results.question: How to setup github repo
results.answer:
You can set up a GitHub repository in several ways:

Option A: Install the GitHub CLI (`gh`) and use it to create the repo:
```powershell
winget install GitHub.cli
```
Then, run this command from inside your project directory:
```powershell
gh repo create notecrate_pipeline --private --source=. --push
```

Option B (via API with curl):
Create a personal access token on github.com/settings/tokens and use it to create the repo via API:
```powershell
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: token YOUR_TOKEN" https://api.github.com/user/repos -d '{\"name\":\"notecrate_pipeline\",\"private\":true}'
```

Option C (via GitHub's web interface): Go to github.com/new, fill in the repository name and other details, and create it.

Note that you already have a .gitignore file committed locally, so don't add another one when creating the remote repository.

results.question: what are the rules or proerties of a red black tree?
results.answer: Every path from a node to its null leaves must contain the same number of black nodes [3]. The root is always allowed to absorb the extra black, so when the double black reaches the root, it simply reduces its color from double black → black [4]. Additionally, every node in the tree has a color (red or black), and there are specific rules for rotations and recoloring to maintain balance [1-5].

results.question: How do you validate whether a tree is a valid red-black tree?

This involves understanding the internal rules of a red-black tree (clear-box reasoning) and validating its behavior through operations rather than inspecting internal variables [2].

results.question: How does building a max heap from an array work?
results.answer:
Building a max-heap from an array can be done in two main ways: inserting elements one by one and percolating up, or using the more efficient method of heapifying an existing array (O(n) time). The standard method is to heapify an existing array. 

To heapify an existing array, start from the last non-leaf node and sift down [3].

results.question: What is the time complexity of heap sort and why?
results.answer: The time complexity of heap sort is O(N log N) [2]. This is because building a heap takes O(N) time, but repeatedly removing max elements and percolating down to restore the heap property dominates the runtime at O(N log N) [4]. The extra O(N) cost of heapifying doesn't change the asymptotic runtime because it's linear work compared to the N log N work of the sorting phase [5].

results.question: What's the difference between clear-box and I/O testing?
results.answer: Clear-box testing uses knowledge of the internal implementation or invariants of a data structure, but can still interact only through public methods [2]. In contrast, an I/O test verifies behavior based on inputs and outputs, not by directly inspecting internal fields [3]. A clear-box test can be both, as it checks internal state (clear-box) while using specific input to observe a specific output (I/O) [3].

results.question: How do taints and tolerations control pod scheduling?
results.answer:
Taints are automatically created by the node controller for certain node conditions, such as `DiskPressure` or `MemoryPressure`, with an effect of `NoSchedule`. This prevents new pods from being scheduled onto affected nodes. Pods can be scheduled onto tainted nodes if they have a matching toleration [1].

The scheduler checks taints when making scheduling decisions, not node conditions themselves. Tolerations allow pods to be scheduled on nodes with matching taints [4]. 

Taints and tolerations are used in various use cases, such as dedicating nodes for exclusive use by particular users or keeping pods that don't need specialized hardware off of nodes with special hardware [6].
